summary: This informational document deprecates any int domain names that the IETF designated for infrastructure and identifies them for removal from the int top-level domain. Implementations involving these domains are now deprecated. It also changes RFC 1528 and RFC 1706 to Historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Some old internet names ending in int were set aside for internet plumbing. This document says stop using them and moves two old documents to the history shelf.

questions: why is the int domain no longer used for infrastructure
what domains were removed from int
subtitle: Retiring old internet infrastructure names from the int domain.

tldr.problem: The int top-level domain was historically used for internet infrastructure purposes, but these experimental uses are now obsolete and should be cleaned up.
tldr.mechanism: This document identifies seven historical int subdomains (atma.int, ip4.int, ip6.int, nsap.int, rdi.int, reg.int, tpc.int) and marks them as deprecated, with their specifications moved to Historic status.
tldr.outcome: The int domain is now reserved solely for intergovernmental treaty organizations, and related RFCs 1528 and 1706 are reclassified as Historic.

facts.value: 7 (atma.int, ip4.int, ip6.int, nsap.int, rdi.int, reg.int, tpc.int)

today: RFC 9121 is an Informational RFC published in April 2023. The int domain is now exclusively for intergovernmental treaty organizations, and all historical infrastructure uses have been formally deprecated and removed from DNS. The arpa domain is the proper home for internet infrastructure identifiers.

sections.title: Why the int Domain Was Cleaned Up
sections.content:
The int top-level domain is a specialized naming space reserved for intergovernmental organizations established by international treaties. However, in the early days of the internet, this domain was also used experimentally for infrastructure purposes—ways the internet plumbing identified itself in the domain name system.

In 2001, RFC 3172 established that the arpa domain was the proper home for such infrastructure identifiers. This policy change meant no new int domains could be created for infrastructure, but the old experimental ones remained. Over time, the organizations using them stopped, and these domains became obsolete. This document formally deprecates them.
sections.plainLanguage: The int domain was an old experimental playground for internet infrastructure names, but it was declared off-limits for that purpose in 2001. Now we are officially closing down the unused old experiments.

sections.title: The Seven Deprecated Domains
sections.content:
The RFC lists seven infrastructure int subdomains that are now deprecated:

  • atma.int — experimental address lookups for Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) end systems
  • ip4.int — an alternative to in-addr.arpa for mapping IPv4 addresses to names (in-addr.arpa is still in use)
  • ip6.int — originally delegated for IPv6 address mapping, but replaced by ip6.arpa and removed from the int zone
  • nsap.int — experimental mapping of Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) Network Service Access Points to domain names
  • rdi.int — experimental mapping of OSI routing domain identifiers
  • reg.int — hosted an experimental mechanism for publishing IANA registration values in DNS
  • tpc.int — hosted an experimental remote printing service bridging email and facsimile transmission

Although each was either delegated or documented at some point, the parties administering them stopped using them long ago.
sections.plainLanguage: There were seven old experimental address systems hidden under the int domain—for ATM, IPv4, IPv6, OSI protocols, and a fax service. None of them work anymore because the organizations that set them up abandoned them decades ago.

sections.title: Security and Cleanup Implications
sections.content:
Some old systems might have these domain names hardwired in their configuration and expect a positive DNS response. However, this is true for any obsolete name in DNS and should not be sufficient reason to keep them. Existing applications should eliminate any reliance on these zones.

The operator of the int domain should be cautious about any potential re-use of these domain names for legitimate intergovernmental treaty organizations, as the old registrations may create confusion or conflicts. The RFC notes that IANA has formally removed all delegations for these historical int domains from the DNS.
sections.plainLanguage: Some very old programs might look for these domains and get confused when they disappear, but that's okay because those programs should have been updated long ago. The cleanup also means nobody can accidentally reuse these names and cause confusion.

sections.title: Formal Status Changes
sections.content:
This document changes the status of two related RFCs to Historic:

  • RFC 1528 (the specification for tpc.int and its remote printing service) is now Historic.
  • RFC 1706 (the specification for nsap.int and DNS NSAP resource records) is now Historic.

The int domain is now reserved exclusively for intergovernmental treaty organizations, and the arpa domain remains the proper home for internet infrastructure identifier spaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Two old instruction manuals for these systems are officially put on the shelf as "history"—they still exist for reference if someone wants to understand what we tried, but they do not describe anything that currently works.
